Problem & Solution

Students don't fail because they're lazy. They fail because they don't see it coming.

Loopin is a personalized planner built for university students — one that pays attention to how each student actually works, and nudges them toward the right task at the right time, before small delays turn into a pile-up.

The ProblemWho Is AffectedMini ResearchWhat Students Told UsThe SolutionWhy It Matters

The Problem

University students juggle deadlines and commitments spread across a handful of disconnected places: an LMS like Canvas or Blackboard, university email, a WhatsApp group for every club and project, a shared calendar, and their own memory. Nothing pulls those pieces together into a single, honest picture of "what does my week actually look like."

The result isn't usually one missed deadline. It's several small delays that quietly stack on top of each other — a reading pushed back a day here, an assignment started a day late there — until they collide on the same Thursday. By the time a student can see the pile-up, it's already too late to spread it out.

Who Is Affected

This affects any university student juggling more than one course, but it's sharpest for students who commute long distances between home and campus, who have less flexible free time in their day than students living on campus, and whose actual "focus hours" rarely match the generic 9-to-5 that most planning tools quietly assume. It also affects students balancing academics with clubs, part-time work, or career prep — anyone whose day isn't just "class, then homework."

Mini Research

Academic procrastination is one of the most consistently documented problems in student life. A meta-analysis published in Psychological Bulletin by researcher Piers Steel estimates that 80–95% of college students procrastinate on their coursework, and that roughly half do so consistently and problematically.

That same research points to a specific cause: procrastination is rarely about laziness. It's more often driven by not knowing where to start, underestimating how a task will grow, or simply not seeing a busy day coming until it arrives.

Source: Steel, P. (2007). "The Nature of Procrastination: A Meta-Analytic and Theoretical Review of Quintessential Self-Regulatory Failure." Psychological Bulletin, 133(1), 65–94. doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.133.1.65

What Students Told Us

Alongside the published research, we asked a small group of university students how they actually manage their workload. This is early, exploratory feedback — two detailed responses so far — not a formal study, but it lined up closely with what we set out to fix.

"I wish it would show everything I should do in one place and tell what task I have to focus on first."— University student, informal interview
"My biggest problem is procrastination. I know what work to do but don't know which one to start first or where to start."— University student, informal interview
"I might have one assignment I'm working on and start worrying about the next assignment, which I haven't started yet."— University student, informal interview
"When I felt overwhelmed I started procrastinating, and it was burdening me."— University student, informal interview

One honest finding worth naming: when asked whether they'd rather get lots of reminders or one clear recommendation, both students said they'd prefer frequent reminders — not the single "one clear nudge" a minimal design might assume is always better. That's not a contradiction we're smoothing over — it's exactly why Setup asks about reminder style directly, instead of deciding for every student what "less noise" should mean.

The Solution

Most planning tools are really just a place to store what's due — a to-do list, a calendar, an LMS. They're honest about what is due, but silent on when a student should actually sit down and do it, or which of five things deserves tonight's hour. That gap — between knowing your workload and knowing your next move — is exactly where the pile-up sneaks in.

Loopin starts with a short Personal Setup instead of waiting weeks to "learn" a student's habits silently. It asks about your program and modules, the assessments you're carrying, when you focus best, what kind of task you tend to put off, how much real free time you have on a busy day, and how you prefer reminders. Every part of the dashboard is then built around those answers.

  • Today — a real schedule of the day's classes, commute, and commitments, so the app understands usable time, not just empty calendar space, plus the task a student is most likely to delay quietly flagged.
  • A Smart Nudge — a specific suggestion for when to do which task today, based on the student's own focus time, actual modules and assessments, and realistic free time — not a generic reminder.
  • Week ahead — a simple 7-day view that makes a coming pile-up visible days in advance, instead of the night before.
  • Weekly insights — honest, module-aware feedback on which nudges were acted on, and which module still needs earlier warning next time.

Nothing about Loopin asks a student to change how they work. It simply makes the shape of their week visible before it becomes a problem.

Why It Matters

Procrastination isn't just a productivity inconvenience — research links it to increased stress and anxiety, and it directly affects grades when multiple deadlines collide. For students who already lose part of their day to commuting between cities, or who are juggling classes, clubs, and part-time work, a scattered week isn't just stressful — it's genuinely harder to recover from once things pile up.

Loopin matters because it treats the real cause of missed deadlines — not seeing the week clearly — as the problem worth solving, instead of adding one more list for students to check.
